messages.subject: Re: three questions about model specifications
messages.body_plain:
1. those are start values. they help the model converge, so they should be sensible given what you know/expect about the data but do not need to be perfect. Some educated guesswork is involved. All models have default start values for all parameters, but in this case we are overriding the defaults to facilitate convergence.
2. this would basically be a standard cholesky approach with more than two variables. if you search for papers from the twin literature (e.g. published in behavior genetics) you should be able to find lots of examples of what a trivariate cholesky looks like.
3. i'm not sure what you mean "due to". In the Demange paper we decompose EA into cognitive and noncognitive components. It sounds like you are interested in both. We do that. Note that the cognitive component is just the cognitive performance GWAS. The only difference is that the betas may be rescaled depending on how you parameterize the model. The supplement to that paper discusses some of the more technical details further. Supp Fig. 17 shows how we correlate both the cog and noncog components with an external GWAS trait.

messages.subject: Re: three questions about model specifications
messages.body_plain:
1. The sqrt of the snp h2 of the trait (taken from the diag of the S matrix) is probably sensible. Or perhaps half or a quarter of that value for a Cholesky cross-path. If you aren’t having convergence issues, you don’t need to worry about this.

2. The lavaan language is flexible and straightforward once you get the hang of it, so you can definitely extend your code to a trivariate Cholesky.

3. There is not a distinction between the genetic effects on cognitive ability and those relevant to the portion of autism attributable to cognitive ability.  It’s the same factor from which two different paths emanate (one pointing to cog ability and one pointing to autism), so the GWAS sumstats for that factor are identical.

messages.subject: Effective Sample Size for Munge
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am performing a common factor GWAS that will involve two continuous traits and two binary traits. For binary trait #1, the sample size is 46,568, and the sample prevalence is 0.284. For binary trait #2, the sample size is 513,497, and the sample prevalence is 0.0418. I just want to confirm that, for munge(), I should use the formula 4v(1-v)n to compute N - thus, N would be specified as 37,877.3 for binary trait #1 and 82,267.9 for binary trait #2?

Thank you all for your help! New user here!

Best wishes,
Mallory

messages.subject: Re: Effective Sample Size for Munge
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mallory,
It depends on whether your binary traits are from a single GWAS or a meta-analysis of GWASs. If a meta analysis you need to use the sum of EffN from each contributing cohort, which is sometimes already provided in the sumstats file itself.
After supplying the correct EffN then you'll input the sample prev as .5 in ldsc().
See
https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.09.22.21263909v1

My CFI is good but the SRMR of my model is quite high (0.13).

Best,

Camille Williams

messages.subject: Re: Sample size for munge function
messages.body_plain:
We have transitioned to recommending that you provide effective sample size and setting the sample prevalence to .5 in LDSC. The introduction to section 3 of the wiki has been edited accordingly.

For single cohort GWAS of binary traits, effect sample size (i.e. the equivalent sample size for a balanced case-control study) is computed as 4(v(1-v))n where v is the true sample prevalence. For summary statistics from a meta-analysis of multiple case-control GWAS, you should use the sum of effective sample sizes.

See the following preprint for further details:

Grotzinger, A. D., de la Fuente, J., Nivard, M. G., & Tucker-Drob, E. M. (2021). Pervasive downward bias in estimates of liability scale heritability in GWAS meta-analysis: A simple solution. medRχiv. Link <https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.09.22.21263909> (to preprint)

messages.subject_clean: Syntax for other multivariate GWAS methods
messages.body_plain:
Several multivariate GWAS methods have been described (eg. MTAG, N-GWAMA, etc). In this video overview of the Genomic SEM method (https://youtu.be/ECwQS5UD3YM?t=2768), a Genomic SEM implementation of the MTAG method is mentioned. Is there example lavaan syntax for implementing this method (eg. for 2+ traits)?

Similarly, how does the common factor approach compare with the N-weighted multivariate GWAMA method reported here: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-018-0320-8 - if different, can this model be specified within Genomic SEM?

Thanks,
-Mike

messages.subject: Re: Syntax for other multivariate GWAS methods
messages.subject_clean: Syntax for other multivariate GWAS methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

The supplement to the original Grotzinger 2019 <http://labs.la.utexas.edu/tucker-drob/files/2019/05/Genomic-SEM-Supplement.pdf> paper provides a formal treatment of how a model equivalent to the MTAG model can be specified within Genomic SEM. In practice, there are a few ways to do this. One way is to regress the target phenotype on the SNP (T ~ SNP) and regress the supporting phenotypes on the target phenotype (Y1 + Y2 +Y3 ~ T). The supporting phenotypes can be allowed to have residual covariances with one another (Y1~~Y2, Y1~~Y3, Y2~~Y3). A second way is to specify a common factor GWAS, forcing the residual variance of the target phenotype to 0, such that the factor is isomorphic with the target phenotype (F ~ SNP, F =~ 1*T + Y1 + Y2 + Y3, T ~~ 0*T). Again, the supporting phenotypes can be allowed to have residual covariances with one another (Y1~~Y2, Y1~~Y3, Y2~~Y3).

With respect to N-weighted multivariate GWAMA, the key assumption is that the contributing GWAS each represent the same phenotype (in practice different genetically correlated GWAS phenotypes can be used, but this is not taken into account), but that they may be differentially precise (hence the N-weighting) and differentially heritable (e.g. due to differences in reliability of the measures used). Note that, like MTAG and Genomic SEM, N-weighted multivariate GWAMA takes (potentially unknown) sample overlap into account. A Genomic SEM model similar to N-weighted multivariate GWAMA would be to create a common factor GWAS with all residual variances of the factor indicators fixed to 0 (F~SNP, F=~ Y1+Y2+Y3, Y1~~0*Y1, Y2~~0*Y2, Y3~~0*Y3). Note that the weighted least squares estimator in Genomic SEM optimizes parameter estimates by weighting by the inverse square of the standard errors of the SNP effects (and genetic covariances) which is similar to N-weighting. To represent a model similar to a standard GWAS meta-analysis that assumes the same phenotype and equal heritabilities, you would further fix all factor loadings to be equal.  This can be done by making them all 1.0 (F =~ 1*Y1 + 1*Y2 + 1*Y3).

Finally, you may be interested in what we have referred to in the Grotzinger et al. (2020)  <https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.09.22.20196089v1>preprint as an unstructured GWAS meta-analysis, which imposes no structure on the expected pattern of associations between the SNPs and the individual GWAS phenotypes. This is similar to the ASSET-based method used for meta-analysis in Lee et al. (2019) <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867419312760>. To conduct an unstructured GWAS meta-analysis, you compare a model in which all phenotypes are regressed onto the SNP (Y1 + Y2 + Y3 ~ SNP) with one in which all of these regressions are fixed to 0 (Y1 + Y2 + Y3 ~ 0*SNP). Residual covariances among the phenotypes can be freely estimated in both models. In other words, you run 2 models per SNP. The difference in chi square statistics between the two models is itself a chi squared distributed test statistic with df equal to the number of GWAS phenotypes. This test statistic quantifies the evidence for an overall effect of the SNP on any subset of the phenotypes, irrespective of the patterning or directionality of the effects.

Best Regards,

Elliot

messages.subject: Re: Sample size for munge function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a follow-up question regarding effective sample size. I have a binary trait from a single cohort but case/control is unbalanced which result in very small sample prevalence and effective sample size.

So when I generate a common factor, the following message pops up.

"A difference greater than .025 was observed pre- and post-smoothing in the genetic covariance matrix. This reflects a large difference and results should be interpreted with caution!! This can often result from including low powered traits, and you might consider removing those traits from the model. If you are going to run a multivariate GWAS we strongly recommend setting the smooth_check argument to true to check smoothing for each SNP."

Is there a way to handle with unbalanced case/control GWAS? (I have checked that if I exclude this trait, the message does not appear.)

Best,
Austin

messages.subject: Re: Sample size for munge function
messages.body_plain:
The method described in the Grotzinger (2021) preprint that I referred to previously accounts for the unbalanced nature of case-control GWAS. The warning that you are getting is not related to whether the GWAS is balanced or not. It refers to the fact that the empirical genetic covariance matrix is nonpositive definite, and that the closest positive definite matrix to the empirical matrix has some elements that are very different front the original. This typically happens when one or more of the GWASs has low power, such that the h2 and rG estimates involving that GWAS are noisy. Indeed, you mention that the case control trait has a low effective N (i.e. low power), and that  when you remove this trait, the warning goes away. While it is true that a case-control with very few cases has low power, even when the total N is large, it is the low power that is relevant, not the unbalanced nature of the GWAS per se.
